title: Insurability Index and Tax-Base Hedge for Towns
one_liner: Measure insurance withdrawal town by town, then hedge municipal property-tax bases against it.
customer: Municipal finance officers of small towns, school districts and special districts in Florida, California and Colorado. Muni bond funds, community banks and rating analysts buy the data.
problem: When insurance leaves, home values fall, the tax base erodes and bonds reprice, yet nobody measures insurability itself. FAIR and Citizens policy counts, nonrenewal filings and rate filings are public but fragmented. Physical-risk scoring is commoditizing (MSCI-First Street), but insurance availability is not measured.
solution: A monthly ZIP and county Insurability Index (FAIR or Citizens share, nonrenewal filings, carrier appetite, premium-to-value), sold to muni investors, community banks and appraisers. In year two, add index-linked parametric tax-base protection backed by ILS capital, paying towns when the index crosses agreed thresholds.
why_now: Cat bonds are at record scale (about $65.6B outstanding with 12 first-time sponsors), FAIR keeps growing, and physical-risk data is consolidating while insurance availability is unmeasured.
revenue_model: $10-50K data subscriptions, then structuring fees and hedge premium.
non_obvious_insight: The financial risk is insurance withdrawal, not physical damage. It is measurable from public regulator data, and municipal budgets are unhedged against it.
first_30_days: Build the index for California and Florida counties from public data. Send it monthly to 20 muni analysts and community bankers, and convert the first subscribers.

title: Rebuild-Cost Audit Sold Through Agents' E&O Fear
one_liner: A 15-minute independent rebuild-cost check at renewal that documents limits, sold to the agents and E&O carriers who hold the underinsurance tail.
customer: Independent agencies in California, Colorado and Florida and their E&O program managers. Wealth advisors and trust attorneys for high-value homes are a second channel.
problem: In the Palisades, insurer estimates run about $462/sq ft against contractor budgets up to $1,065, and only about 13% of owners have started rebuilding. Part of that gap is contractor premium, but a large part is stale valuation. Owners are underinsured, and the agents who sold the limits carry E&O exposure. Renewals in 2026-27 are the moment to fix it.
solution: A rebuild reality check that pulls permit records, local bid data, post-disaster cost surge and home features. It outputs a defensible range and recommended limits or extended replacement cost, with contractor validation for the top decile of homes. It is white-labeled by the agent, and the audit log doubles as an E&O defense file.
why_now: The LA fire claims experience is now public and quantified, so E&O carriers and agencies finally have a concrete loss to point at.
revenue_model: $29-99 per policy to the agency, or a program fee from an E&O carrier that gives premium credits. A $299 tier adds a contractor walk-through.
non_obvious_insight: The economic buyer is not the homeowner but the agent's E&O carrier, who wants documentation. Underinsurance is the biggest unpriced tail left after the LA fires.
first_30_days: Calibrate on 100 posted Palisades and Altadena claim outcomes. Pitch 5 agencies with high-value books, and approach one agency E&O program manager about a documented-audit premium credit.

title: Texas Data-Center Water Filing and Attestation
one_liner: A fixed-fee compliance service that meters, calculates, files and PE-attests data-center water reports for the operators who ignored Texas's mandatory water survey.
customer: About 280 non-responding Texas data centers (colos, crypto miners, enterprise sites, edge facilities) and developers of the roughly 1,800 projects held in the ERCOT queue. The operator or developer pays.
problem: Only 17% of 341 surveyed Texas data centers answered the mandatory 2025 water survey (maximum fine $500). On Aug 3 the governor froze ERCOT connection approvals pending a water and energy audit, and TWDB owes an update by Oct 14, 2026. Non-reporting is about to become a crime and a bar to TCEQ permits and interconnection. Small operators have no in-house water or regulatory staff.
solution: A turnkey filing: interpret the survey, verify or install non-invasive clamp-on flow metering on make-up and blowdown lines, reconcile utility bills, compute WUE plus scarcity-adjusted and grid-indirect water, then have a Texas licensed PE sign an attestation. Keep an audit-ready data room and issue quarterly updates as rules change.
why_now: The freeze, the Oct 14 update and the coming criminal penalties all land within weeks. A stamp from an independent PE unblocks permits and interconnection, and nobody else sells it to the long tail.
revenue_model: $5-15k per-facility filing package, $2-5k/month recurring attestation, $50-200k portfolio deals. Anonymized data becomes the first scarcity-adjusted benchmark set.
non_obvious_insight: The hyperscalers will self-certify. The 83% who did not respond, mostly small and mid-size operators, will be the first enforcement targets. Enforcement demand arrives suddenly, and whoever has met 50 operators and installed 50 meters in the first wave owns the reference dataset.
first_30_days: Build a list of Texas data centers from public survey and ERCOT queue records. Partner with a Texas engineering firm for PE stamps. Host a 'what to do before Oct 14' webinar, cold-email 100 non-responders, and close the first five filings at $5-10k.

title: Contingency Recovery of Missed Rotable Repair Warranties
one_liner: A success-fee auditor that finds repaired aircraft components that failed inside the shop's warranty window, and turns them into filed claims and cash.
customer: Small and mid-size operators with their own stores and a thin materials team. That means regional airlines, Part 135 cargo feeders and air-ambulance fleets, and Part 145 shops that buy their own exchange units. They pay 20-25% of whatever cash or credit is recovered, and nothing up front.
problem: A repaired starter-generator, bleed valve, hydraulic pump or fuel control that fails 4 months after the shop visit is often covered by warranty. Almost nobody claims it. The tech pulling the unit at 3 AM is trying to make a 6 AM departure and never sees the warranty terms. The repair invoice sits in accounts payable as a PDF. The removal record sits in the maintenance system, and hours and cycles sit in a third place. One materials coordinator owns thousands of removals a year, with 30-90 day claim windows. Three other leaks go unclaimed as well: 'no fault found' evaluation fees on units that were still under warranty, unreturned exchange cores that turn into penalty charges, and repair turnaround-time guarantees that shops never credit because nobody compares PO date to receipt date.
solution: Ingest three exports: removals and installs, PO and repair invoices (PDFs read with an LLM extractor), and the negotiated warranty terms. Match by part number and serial number, including interchangeable P/Ns. Flag every in-warranty failure, late repair turn, disputable NFF fee and open core. Then draft the claim on each vendor's own template, track it to a paid credit, and re-run monthly. Add a 3 AM 'is this unit under warranty?' lookup for maintenance control, so the claim gets started at the moment of removal.
why_now: Airline cost pressure on regionals is high, and mechanic wages rose sharply in 2024-2026, so labor cost per removal is up. Materials teams are being cut while fleets stay old. LLM invoice and PDF extraction only became reliable and cheap enough in the last 18 months, and that is the missing link, because the money sits in unstructured AP documents that MRO software never reads.
revenue_model: Contingency fee of 20-25% of recovered cash and credits, with a 12-month tail on the audit. Later add a $2-5k per month SaaS tier for continuous monitoring, and sell benchmark data on shop warranty behavior to airline procurement teams.
non_obvious_insight: The leak is not in the maintenance system, it is in accounts payable. The tech who removes the part, the coordinator who could file the claim and the department that paid the invoice never share a screen. MRO software vendors will not fix it because warranty terms live in negotiated PDFs, not fields. Repair shops know most eligible claims are never filed, and they price that into their rates. A contingency auditor is the same playbook as freight-audit and telecom-audit firms, aimed at a niche nobody has covered.
first_30_days: Pitch 10 directors of maintenance and materials managers at small regionals, cargo feeders and helicopter EMS operators. Offer a free 12-month leakage audit, and ask them for the three exports. Build the matcher in Python plus an LLM invoice parser, and use a retired warranty or materials coordinator as a paid advisor for vendor quirks. Deliver a ranked claim list to the first 2-3 customers, file the claims yourself, and sign the success-fee agreement on the first credit memo. Publish the aggregate audit finding, such as the percentage of eligible failures that were never claimed, as the lead magnet.

title: Reuse Exchange for Closing Parish Contents
one_liner: A cataloging, canon-law compliance and matching service that moves stained glass, statues, vestments, bells and furniture from closing parishes to churches that need them.
customer: Dioceses and archdiocesan closure committees, religious orders and denominational property offices, with receiving parishes, new chapels and immigrant or missionary congregations on the other side.
problem: Closure committees catalog contents by hand, and surplus goes out through liturgical dealers. Sacred items risk profane use (confessionals turned into restaurant phone booths, upsetting donors' families), canon law restricts profane sale, and organs and murals often cannot be saved.
solution: A photo-cataloging app with AI-assisted identification, provenance and donor-plaque tracking, blessed-status and canon-law flags, and a bishop approval workflow. A gated marketplace of vetted receiving churches, including overseas missions served by consolidated containers. Optionally digitally sample condemned organs before removal.
why_now: Parish consolidations continue while church attendance is flat (Pew: 33% attend monthly). Dioceses are cash-strapped and want revenue from contents. Photo AI and container consolidation are now cheap.
revenue_model: A per-closure project fee ($5-25k), 10-15% commission on sales, and a freight-consolidation margin on overseas shipments.
non_obvious_insight: Buyers are not the scarce input. Trust and compliance are: sellers need proof items will not be profaned, and buyers in growing regions need provenance and affordable freight. A vetted receiving-church network is the asset incumbents (liturgical dealers) lack.
first_30_days: Offer 3 diocesan property offices a free catalog of one closing church. Build a list of 50 missionary and immigrant-parish buyers through religious-order mission offices. Ship the first container.

title: Verified Pay Receipts for Truck Driver Hiring
one_liner: Drivers upload settlement stubs and AI turns them into the true, receipts-backed pay per mile and per hour away from home for every carrier, sold as a hiring credential and as income proof for lenders.
customer: Honest mid-size carriers (50 to 1,000 trucks) that pay $6k to $15k to hire each driver and can't prove their pay claims are real. Secondary buyers are mortgage and auto lenders (bank-statement and non-QM brokers) who serve drivers.
problem: Recruiter ads say 'up to 75 cents a mile, $100k+' but realized pay is often 20 to 35% lower after unpaid or practical-versus-paid miles, unpaid detention, chargebacks and deductions. Driver turnover at big truckload carriers runs near 90%, and job ads are so discredited that honest carriers can't stand out. Drivers whose pay is structured as tax-free 'per diem' also see a low W-2 and get denied mortgages after 20 years of work. Estimates say the English-proficiency and non-domiciled CDL crackdowns will pull 214,000 to 437,000 drivers (5 to 12% of CDL holders) from the supply over 2 to 3 years, so carriers are competing harder for domestic drivers.
solution: A mobile app where drivers photograph settlement stubs and pay statements. AI extracts paid miles, deadhead, detention, deductions, per diem and time away from home, and computes effective take-home per hour on the road, not just per mile. Public carrier pages show verified figures such as '312 verified drivers, median $0.61 per paid mile, $17.40 per hour away'. Carriers that look good pay for a 'Verified Pay' badge and applicant funnel. A second product builds an income-verification packet from stubs and deposit statements for lenders. Fraud controls include stub-format checks, duplicate detection and consistency with driver-reported miles.
why_now: Shrinking driver supply from the 2025 to 2026 English-proficiency out-of-service enforcement (proposed codification rule published Aug 10, 2026) and the Feb 2026 non-domiciled CDL restrictions means cost-per-hire is rising. Vision-model OCR of messy pay stubs is now cheap and accurate. Truth-in-leasing rules already require itemized settlements, so the raw material exists.
revenue_model: Carrier subscriptions of $500 to $3,000 a month for the verified page, analytics and applicant funnel. Lender referral fees of $300 to $1,000 per funded mortgage or truck loan. Free for drivers, which keeps the data supply growing.
non_obvious_insight: Drivers don't compare carriers by ads, they ask in the truck-stop lot 'what do you actually clear?' The only artifact they trust is a pay stub. The honest carriers are the ones locked out of trust, so they are the natural paying customer. The true unit of pay is dollars per hour away from home, because 14-hour clocks, detention and unpaid waiting eat the mileage math. And per-diem income structures are a hidden mortgage trap that a stub-based income packet can fix.
first_30_days: Post in trucker Facebook groups, Reddit and TikTok: 'Upload your stub, see your real rate vs. what your carrier advertised.' Aim for 500 stubs in 30 days. Publish a 'State of Real Pay' report ranking 20 named carriers and pitch it to trade press (Overdrive, CDLLife, FreightWaves). Sell 'Verified Pay' badges to the 5 mid-size fleets whose numbers look best, and sign one bank-statement mortgage broker for lender leads.

title: Router-and-Breaker Screen Control Sold by Trades
one_liner: HVAC, electrical and plumbing shops install tamper-proof, infrastructure-level screen and AI-companion controls as a maintenance-plan add-on for families with kids 8-15.
customer: Home-service shops with 5-30 techs and a maintenance-plan base (they resell the kit), and the parents of 8-15-year-olds who pay $199-349 to install plus $12-18 a month. Slow-season HVAC shops are the first wave.
problem: Under-16 social bans and school phone rules leak: VPNs cost under A$20 a month, seven in ten Australian under-16s reportedly still hold accounts, and only 29% of parents planned full compliance. App-level controls live on the device the kid controls, so they get uninstalled, and they cannot touch consoles, smart TVs, AI toys or AI companion sites. Parents want enforcement kids cannot delete. Meanwhile HVAC shipments fell 25-50% and shops have idle techs and a need for recurring revenue.
solution: A standard 'family network' kit installed in one visit, built from a hardwired or mesh router with router-level policies (VPN and proxy blocking, AI-companion and social categories by age tier, per-device schedules, guest SSID), plus smart-relay outlets ('kid circuits') for consoles and TVs, and a phone-parking charging nook. Parents manage it in a simple app, and shops get a two-hour training course and a quarterly tune-up visit. Cellular data is honestly disclosed as out of scope, and the kit aims at evenings and nights at home.
why_now: Bans and age-assurance rules are live in Australia, Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Texas and Ohio, and Australia is proposing to double fines, so enforcement is the gap. The FTC's 2025 6(b) inquiry and state AI-companion laws put AI chatbots at the center of parental worry. HVAC is at a trough until a 2027 rebound, so shops want add-on services now.
revenue_model: Hardware-plus-install margin split with shops (about $75 spiff plus 30-40% of install), $12-18 per household per month recurring, and training and certification fees for shops.
non_obvious_insight: Software controls sit on the device kids control, so enforcement has to move to infrastructure parents physically own, and installing infrastructure is a trades skill. A local HVAC shop with 2,000 plan customers, most of them families, has near-zero customer acquisition cost compared with consumer parental-control apps.
first_30_days: Build the kit on off-the-shelf router hardware with DNS and VPN filtering and smart relays. Train two local electrical or HVAC shops and pilot 20 installs with a $75 spiff. Log bypass attempts and parent satisfaction, then sign five more shops using the pilot's numbers.

title: Safe-Deposit Box Successor With Heir Protocol
one_liner: A bonded, insured vault subscription for original wills, deeds, titles, seed-phrase backups and heirlooms, with a scripted release protocol for heirs, sold through estate attorneys as the bank box disappears.
customer: Estate-planning and elder-law attorneys as the channel, and their clients aged 55 to 85 whose plan says 'the original is in the safe deposit box'. Secondary: coin, gold and crypto holders, and small landlords and business owners holding original deeds and titles.
problem: Chase said in August 2025 that it would phase out all remaining safe deposit boxes nationwide, after it stopped new rentals in 2021. Capital One, Santander and Citizens exited earlier, and the total number of boxes has reportedly fallen from about 40M to an estimated 25M to 32M. Contents are not FDIC-insured, and no federal law governs boxes. On a death the bank typically freezes access until paperwork clears. The box was the default chain of custody for the paper that proves who owns what, and nothing has replaced it.
solution: Rent standardized boxes or sealed envelopes inside licensed, bonded vault partners. Each item gets a photo and hash inventory, and contents are insured under a valuables policy. The core product is a designated-heir protocol: on a death certificate plus an attorney letter or executor's letters, the vault releases to the named person after video attestation and dual control. Add periodic proof-of-life check-ins, an index the attorney can see, and an original-will custody service tied to the attorney's office.
why_now: Chase's nationwide phase-out (announced August 2025) removed the largest holder of boxes. The Great Wealth Transfer is under way. Retail gold and crypto holdings create new 'irreplaceable original' items such as seed backups and coins that people do not want in a home closet.
revenue_model: $15 to $35 per month per box, or $199 to $399 per year. A $99 onboarding and inventory fee. A $250 heir-release fee. A white-label or referral share of $5 to $10 per client per month for law firms. Margin on the insurance premium.
non_obvious_insight: The box was never about valuables. It was legal chain of custody for original paper, and banks are quitting because vault space is expensive real estate, not because the need went away. The product is the death protocol that banks never offered, since banks freeze access and a vault plus an attorney workflow can release to the named heir within days. Attorneys are the distribution because they carry malpractice risk when originals are lost.
first_30_days: Check whether your state regulates safe-deposit companies, then sign a white-label deal with one existing bonded vault or secure records-storage operator in a single metro. Draft the release protocol and client agreement with two estate attorneys. Present to 5 estate-planning firms and one senior center with a free 'Where are your originals?' inventory worksheet as the lead magnet. Sell 30 founding-member boxes at a discounted annual rate and run the first two mock heir releases to prove the protocol.

title: Cross-Mine Critical Spares Pool and Inventory Cleanup
one_liner: An AI cleaner for mine SAP materials masters that frees cash from duplicate spares, then turns the informal WhatsApp groups of competing mines' maintenance planners into a contractual, insured rotables pool for mill motors, liners and haul-truck parts.
customer: Supply chain, maintenance and finance heads at mid-size copper and lithium operations, starting in clusters where operators are neighbours: Arizona, Nevada and Utah, Antofagasta, the Arequipa-Moquegua corridor, the Zambian Copperbelt and the Pilbara. They pay a share of freed cash, not an IT budget.
problem: A copper mine holds $30-150M of spares. Materials masters are full of duplicates and near-duplicates (the same bearing under five descriptions), often 20-30% of items, so mines overbuy what is on another shelf. They still stock out on truly critical items (mill drive motors, girth gears, transformers, big castings) with 12-24 month lead times. Meanwhile maintenance planners across competing companies already borrow parts from each other over WhatsApp groups. It works only among friends and has no contracts, insurance, condition guarantees or return terms, so it never scales.
solution: Step one is the wedge. A CSV export of the SAP MM data goes into an LLM pipeline with OEM and aftermarket cross-references, multilingual description normalisation and criticality scoring. It outputs a list of duplicates, surplus and dead stock, plus the freed working capital in dollars. Step two lists surplus and 'insurance spares' on a members-only district board with a standard loan, lease and sale agreement, third-party condition inspection (vibration, NDT), logistics and insurance. It works like airline rotable pooling: three neighbouring mines share one spare mill motor instead of each stocking one.
why_now: Large motors, transformers and castings have longer lead times because of grid and data-centre demand. Steel and copper tariffs make replacement parts pricier. Lithium mines are cash-starved after the price bust, and copper mines face cost inflation and grade decline, so CFOs are hunting working capital. LLMs can now normalise messy multilingual part descriptions at almost no cost, which was not economic three years ago.
revenue_model: 15-25% of freed cash (sales and avoided purchases only, not write-offs), a pool membership subscription ($1-3k per month), and an 8-10% transaction fee on pooled loans and sales, plus inspection and certification fees.
non_obvious_insight: The spares problem is legal and trust-based, not a software problem. The informal swap network is the real supply chain. The biggest saving is not selling dead stock, it is not buying the 'insurance spare' a neighbour already owns. Pooling is an aviation idea that mining has never adopted because competitors will not share data without a neutral third party.
first_30_days: Through ex-colleagues, offer a free 2-week scan of SAP MM exports (CSV) at two or three mid-size mines. Deliver a dollar value of duplicates and surplus and a target list. Sign a success-fee agreement with the first one that shows a big number. In parallel, seed a private 'list before you buy' board among 20 maintenance planners in one district using Signal or WhatsApp, to formalise the network before any software is built.

title: Pre-Cut Electrical Kits Per House Plan
one_liner: A regional kitting shop ships each production home's wiring as pre-cut, labeled, bundled kits so a helper pulls and a journeyman only terminates and inspects.
customer: Electrical subcontractors serving production and spec builders (5-100 homes a year), and builders in data-center-hot markets such as Texas.
problem: Data centers absorb electricians (nearly a third of the shortage; journeymen on overtime gross $130-170K, vendor stat), and Texas builders report electrical delays of up to 2 months. Meanwhile much rough-in time goes to measuring, cutting and pulling, which does not need a licensed person's minutes.
solution: For each repeat plan, generate a wire schedule and build kits: cable pre-cut and labeled by room and circuit, boxes pre-assembled, home runs pre-bundled, panel schedule pre-printed, delivered in numbered bins by phase. Lower-skill pullers or apprentices do most of the rough-in under supervision, and the journeyman terminates and inspects.
why_now: Electrician arbitrage from data-center overtime, builders with idle houses waiting on electrical, and digital plan libraries that expose structured circuit data. Wire-processing machines are cheap and used equipment is plentiful.
revenue_model: Materials plus 15-25%, or $2-4K per home, with a share of labor savings. Licensing the process to kitting shops in other metros.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource is journeyman minutes on tasks a journeyman does not need to do. Commercial contractors have prefabbed for decades, but residential never did because labor was cheap, and now the ROI is large.
first_30_days: Pick one production builder's most repeated plan. Hire an ex-electrician estimator and buy or rent a used cut-and-label machine. Sell kits for five homes to the builder's electrical sub and measure hours saved per house.

title: Fee-Free Hire Receipts for Migrant Workers
one_liner: A worker-held credential proving a migrant was recruited without fees and paid as contracted, sold to suppliers and brands that must prove no forced labour, and portable to the worker's next job.
customer: Tier-1 suppliers and their EU-facing brand buyers in electronics, garments, construction, hospitality and palm oil. Ethical recruitment agencies are a channel, and the worker is the holder.
problem: From 14 December 2027 the EU Forced Labour Regulation bans products made with forced labour, and importers must prove a negative. Audits are sampled snapshots that are easy to game. Workers in corridors such as Nepal to Malaysia or the Philippines to the Gulf often pay illegal recruitment fees that create debt bondage, and they leave with no portable record of employment or skills.
solution: A WhatsApp-first Hire Receipt. At contract signing the worker gets a signed record of recruiter, employer, wage, contract terms and fees paid (zero, or reimbursed). On arrival there is a passport-custody check, then monthly wage-receipt confirmations. Short translated voice check-ins provide independent verification. The worker holds the credential and shares it on consent with employers and brands, which see aggregate dashboards. Over time it accrues employment history and endorsements usable for the next placement or a remittance-backed loan.
why_now: Law firms published compliance roadmaps for the regulation in September 2026, and brands are starting to build supplier evidence programs 15 months before enforcement. Recruitment-fee evidence is the hardest part to get, and no one holds it continuously.
revenue_model: $10-25 per hire paid by the employer or brand, per-site dashboard subscriptions, and placement referral fees from ethical recruiters later.
non_obvious_insight: Compliance buyers must prove a negative, and only worker-side records can do that. Audits fail because they sample, while a worker-held receipt makes evidence continuous, cheaper and self-enforcing. Because the same credential improves the worker's mobility, the worker's incentives align with the buyer's.
first_30_days: Partner with two ethical recruiters in one corridor and one EU-facing supplier. Pilot for 200 hires using a WhatsApp bot rather than an app. Charge a $5k pilot fee plus a per-hire fee, and write up the evidence pack in the format a brand's compliance team will accept.

title: Program Survival Analytics for Regional Universities
one_liner: A subscription that tells provosts which degree programs will fail the new federal earnings tests and loan-cap economics as AI hollows out their feeder occupations, with a redesign playbook.
customer: Provosts, institutional research offices and deans at regional universities, master's-heavy colleges and online providers ($20-60k a year), plus state systems.
problem: As I understand the 2025 budget law (verify specifics), programs whose graduates don't out-earn benchmarks can lose loan eligibility, and Grad PLUS ended for new borrowers with new caps from July 2026. Graduate programs in cognitive fields (analytics, MBA, MS CS, communications) rely on borrowing, while entry-level demand is falling (NY Fed: 42% recent-grad underemployment). Institutions see it only when enrollment drops.
solution: A program-level model combining College Scorecard earnings, occupation-level job-posting trends, AI-exposure scores and enrollment and borrowing data. It delivers early-warning flags, a scenario tool, recommended pivots (in-degree apprenticeships, short credentials, employer co-design) backed by real employer demand signals, and board-ready compliance reporting.
why_now: The new loan and accountability rules began July 2026, the AI-driven junior hiring freeze is measurable (Stanford: 19% gap for ages 22-25), and university budgets are tight.
revenue_model: Annual licence of $20-60k, program-redesign consulting and state-system contracts.
non_obvious_insight: Universities already face compliance deadlines, but nobody has tied AI exposure to the earnings-test math. A federal deadline creates budget urgency that 'future of work' advice never gets. The first programs to fail are likely master's degrees in cognitive fields.
first_30_days: Build the model from public Scorecard data for ~200 institutions as a proof. Generate 'programs at risk' reports for 20 target universities' master's programs and email institutional-research directors and provosts. Sell three $7.5k pilot diagnostics.

title: Josephine Reborn: Permit Concierge for Home Kitchens
one_liner: Josephine's home-cooked-meal marketplace was boxed in by health law; California's MEHKO law now licenses home restaurants, so build the permit concierge and a compliant direct-to-consumer storefront, not another marketplace.
customer: Home cooks, especially immigrant and regional-cuisine specialists (tamales, Armenian, Korean, Oaxacan, Filipino), in Los Angeles County and the roughly 19 California jurisdictions that had authorized MEHKOs as of May 2026. Many already sell via Instagram and WhatsApp without a permit.
problem: MEHKO caps are 30 meals/day, 90/week and roughly $107k/year. Applying costs about $597 plus about $347/yr in LA County, plus food-handler certification, menu SOPs, labels, sales logs and inspections. Third-party delivery apps are restricted, so cooks cannot just list on DoorDash. No tool enforces the caps, produces inspector-ready records, or helps neighbors find them, and paperwork is mostly in English.
solution: A permit concierge ($249-399 one-time) that completes the application, SOPs and multilingual allergen labels. Then a $20/mo cook operating system: link-in-bio storefront with pre-orders and pickup windows, automatic sell-out at 30/day and 90/week, temperature and sales logs exported in the county's format, and Stripe payments. Demand comes from neighborhood 'Friday drop' maps and newsletters and workplace pickup clusters. Cooks own their customers; there is no marketplace.
why_now: MEHKO adoption is spreading county by county (17 counties plus Berkeley and Long Beach by May 2026), with LA County running an active program. Restaurant prices are high, social commerce is normal, and AI makes multilingual SOPs and labels nearly free. A few early MEHKO startups exist, so the opening is to be permit-first, multilingual and neighborhood-by-neighborhood.
revenue_model: $249-399 permit concierge fee; $20/mo per cook SaaS; roughly 1% payments margin; affiliate income from food-handler training and liability insurance. Later, a bulk-permitting contract with counties that want cleaner inspection records.
non_obvious_insight: The marketplace was the illegal or unscalable part, and under MEHKO it is structurally limited to direct-to-consumer sales. The scarce asset is the permit, and the winning product is compliance and storefront tooling that turns each cook into her own licensed restaurant. Enforcing the meal caps in software becomes a feature, and it makes the vendor the county health department's preferred partner.
first_30_days: Attend LA County MEHKO office hours. Find 10 cooks on Instagram (#lahomecook, #tamales) and do their applications free in exchange for case studies. Build the storefront with Shopify or Stripe plus a no-code cap rule. Target 5 issued permits within about 60 days, then start charging the $20/mo.

title: Portable MRI Vans for Alzheimer's Drug Safety Monitoring
one_liner: A mobile low-field MRI service that scans anti-amyloid patients at home or in memory-care communities for brain-swelling safety checks.
customer: Memory clinics, neurology practices and infusion centers running anti-amyloid therapy, plus health systems. Later, manufacturer patient-support programs and payers.
problem: Anti-amyloid drugs require serial MRI safety monitoring for ARIA (brain swelling or bleeding). Scheduling MRI slots is a hidden throttle, and frail 80-year-olds struggle with hospital scanner visits. With blood tests and at-home dosing widening the funnel, monitoring capacity is the next bottleneck.
solution: A tech plus a portable FDA-cleared low-field scanner (Hyperfine Swoop class) in a van or cart, with teleradiology reads scheduled around dosing. Start with a concordance study against 3T for ARIA-E and ARIA-H (early reports suggest low-field can flag such changes, but it needs validation), then contract per scan to clinics.
why_now: Leqembi Q1 sales rose 74% to $168M, with Eisai and Biogen expecting over $1B this year, a subcutaneous at-home starting dose is now cleared, and two blood tests are cleared. Portable MRI and AI reconstruction have matured.
revenue_model: Per-scan fee of about $250-450 paid by clinics or manufacturer support programs, a per-patient monitoring program subscription, and data licensing for post-marketing studies.
non_obvious_insight: The market talks about drug and diagnosis, but scan capacity and patient logistics decide throughput. The regulatory and reimbursement path is uncertain, so the study itself is the first product and creates the evidence moat.
first_30_days: Contact five memory clinics with anti-amyloid volume, lease a portable scanner, design a 40-patient concordance study with an IRB and neuroradiologists, and ask the drug makers' patient-support programs for pilot funding.

title: Consolidation Shock Radar for Independent Clinics
one_liner: Every roll-up creates a wave of unhappy clients and departing staff near the acquired clinic; sell independents, would-be founders and lenders a radar that finds those neighborhoods first.
customer: Independent and affordable-care clinics (client win-back and recruiting), DVMs leaving corporate to open practices, and practice lenders or equipment lessors.
problem: GoodVets is buying WellHaven (75 to 116 locations, announced 2026-09-24), and Mars runs about 2,100 clinics. After a deal, prices, hours and staffing change, but nearby independents have no signal about where clients and staff are becoming loose. De novo founders pick sites by gut feel and lenders lack local competitive data.
solution: Track acquisitions using state facility records, Google Business Profile and website changes ('now part of...'), price-list scrapes, review-sentiment shifts and job-posting churn. Deliver (a) an alert plus a ready-to-send 'neighbor clinic' welcome campaign and records-transfer kit for independents within 5 miles, (b) recruiting lists of departing DVMs and techs, and (c) site-scoring reports for lenders and de novo founders.
why_now: Continuous roll-ups (GoodVets/WellHaven this week), visits reportedly falling three years running, and corporate chains structurally unable to cut price. Open web data plus LLM extraction makes the tracking cheap for a two-person team.
revenue_model: $199-499 per month per clinic by radius, $2-5K per de novo site report, and a lender API subscription.
non_obvious_insight: Consolidation is discussed as a scale story. The neglected consequence is local displacement: the buyer's own integration changes service and pricing at a known date, which opens a recurring window for competitors. That window is a sellable time-series signal nobody packages.
first_30_days: Build scrapers for 3 states. Identify 30 clinics acquired in the last 12 months. Cold-email 100 independents within 5 miles with a 'your neighborhood's acquired clinics' one-pager. Aim to sell 5 subscriptions at $299 per month.

title: Tariff Refund Claim Files for Small Importers
one_liner: Turn a small importer's messy customs data into a refund-ready, financeable claim ledger, paid by success fee or on sale of the claim.
customer: US importers of record with roughly $50K to $5M of IEEPA duties who lack in-house customs staff, plus the licensed customs brokers serving them. Claim-buying funds and lenders are the second payer, paying a per-file diligence fee.
problem: The Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs in February 2026 and the CIT ordered refunds. CBP's CAPE tool has accepted about $134.7B of the roughly $166B pool as of September 11, 2026. The tail sits with the smallest importers. Their ACE accounts are unapproved, they missed the 90-day request window, or their entries are liquidated beyond the 80-day reprocessing window, which the DOJ is appealing at the Federal Circuit. Phase 3, for liquidated entries, was slated for October 6 but delayed. Many are selling claims at deep discounts out of fear or confusion.
solution: Ingest ACE entry-summary reports, broker CSVs and payment records. Map every line to the IEEPA HTS 9903 lines. Compute per-entry phase eligibility, liquidation dates and protest deadlines. Flag duplicate or wrong importer-of-record entries, drawback and FTZ overlaps, and interest owed. Output CAPE-ready batches plus a chain-of-title 'claim data room' with a probability-weighted value for the appeal-dependent entries. A licensed broker partner files, so the product stays software plus workflow. The same engine reprocesses future tariff refunds and exclusions.
why_now: The window is open now: CAPE phases run through fall 2026, the Federal Circuit appeal will set the value of the liquidated tail, and hedge funds and lenders are already buying refund claims. Successor tariffs under other statutes create the same entry-level data problem next year.
revenue_model: 8 to 12% success fee on refunds recovered. A 2 to 4% origination fee when a claim is sold or financed. $500 to $2,000 per-claim diligence files sold to buyers. A subscription for customs brokers who use it across their book.
non_obvious_insight: Distressed-claims desks (Lehman, FTX, Celsius trade claims) know a claim's price is set less by the underlying merits than by documentation quality, chain of title and timing. Whoever standardizes the data room becomes the market's gatekeeper. The small-importer tail is mispriced because sellers can't prove what they are owed, and buyers can't underwrite what they can't verify. The moat is the underwriting file, not the filing.
first_30_days: Build an ES-003 and ACE CSV parser with two or three friendly licensed customs brokers. Offer a free 'refund gap audit' to 30 small importers found through public importer lists. Sign 10 on contingency. Get letters of intent from one or two claim buyers wanting standardized diligence files.

title: Recurring-Gift Migration Concierge for Churches
one_liner: A fixed-fee service that moves a church's recurring donors off an expensive or hostile giving platform without losing them.
customer: Churches of 100-2,000 weekly attendees paying Pushpay, Subsplash, Tithe.ly or Ministry Brands. The buyer is the pastor, executive pastor or volunteer treasurer.
problem: Recurring gifts are the hostage. Donors' saved cards and bank accounts live inside the incumbent platform, and cancelling is punished. A Pushpay reviewer says the church is 'locked into paying $350/mo for nothing since we've migrated over to the new giving platform.' A Subsplash reviewer reports 'nearly $500 just to stop their services.' Another Subsplash reviewer, on Feb 1, 2026, says they were billed and overdrawn after trying to cancel before the 1/31 renewal. A Tithe.ly app reviewer, on Jul 2, 2026, says the company keeps debiting the account after it was closed. Another Tithe.ly reviewer says there is no way to refund a transaction sent to the wrong place.
solution: Six steps. (1) A free fee audit: upload 3 processor statements and get the effective rate, hidden monthly minimums and the card-versus-ACH mix. (2) Run the PCI-compliant card-on-file transfer to a lower-cost processor. Stripe documents this import path, which needs the old processor to release the data and can take days to weeks. (3) Run a text and email campaign that gets each donor to re-enroll in one tap when their data cannot transfer. (4) Send the cancellation notices in writing at the right time and get confirmation of no further debits. (5) Run a 90-day watch for double billing and stray debits. (6) Add ongoing recovery of failed recurring gifts.
why_now: Reviews dated 2025-2026 show AI-only support and billing disputes across the major church giving vendors. Tithe.ly reviewers cite 'an AI bot only' and a chatbot that 'freezes up'. Stripe has made bulk card-data imports a documented process, so the technical barrier is lower than it was. Year-end giving season is the peak, so churches decide in Q4 and switch in January to avoid splitting the annual giving statement year.
revenue_model: A fixed migration fee of $1,500-$4,000 per church, or 25% of the first year's verified fee savings. A $49/month giving-health add-on that retries failed recurring gifts and flags stray debits. Possible processor partner revenue, disclosed to the church.
non_obvious_insight: Churches are not stuck because the software is good. They are stuck because moving donors looks impossible, and vendors profit from that fear. The technical part is solved, since Stripe documents importing cards and ACH from a prior processor at https://docs.stripe.com/get-started/data-migrations/pan-import. What is missing is a human to run donor communications and paperwork. Evidence: Pushpay ($350/month lock-in after migrating, sales promises that differ from the contract) at https://www.trustpilot.com/review/pushpay.com. Subsplash (about $500 exit penalty, overdraft after cancellation, $800 stuck 'pending') at https://www.trustpilot.com/review/subsplash.com. Tithe.ly (debits after closure, no refund path for errors) at https://itunes.apple.com/us/rss/customerreviews/id=694740700/sortby=mostrecent/xml and https://www.trustpilot.com/review/tithe.ly. Church administrators also trade advice in denominational networks and Facebook groups, so a good migration spreads by word of mouth cheaply.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: build the fee-audit calculator as a spreadsheet plus a landing page, and pull the public Pushpay, Subsplash and Tithe.ly reviewers. Days 10-20: offer 20 churches the free audit through church-admin Facebook groups and denominational finance offices. Days 20-30: sign 2-3 pilot churches for a January migration and pre-sell in Q4. Confirm with a payments attorney that the transfer flow keeps the service out of PCI scope, meaning it never touches card numbers.

title: Advancement Ledger for Parents Funding Jobless Kids
one_liner: A living ledger plus a state-specific estate addendum that records what Boomer parents advance to struggling adult children, so the inheritance later comes out fair and siblings do not end up in court.
customer: Parents aged 65-80 with $500K-$5M estates and two or more adult children, at least one of whom is unemployed or underemployed. Channel: estate attorneys, elder-law firms and RIAs, who white-label it. Payers: parents ($199 setup plus $12-20/mo), firms ($500/mo white label) or RIAs (per-household fee).
problem: The AI hiring freeze (NY Fed: recent-grad underemployment about 42%) turns Mom and Dad into the bank of last resort. Rent, tuition, car and 'bridge loans' flow unevenly to siblings, undocumented and undecided as gift, loan or advancement against inheritance. Decades later, executors and trustees face contested history and estate litigation, and families break. Wealth advisors say family meetings are essential, yet nobody tracks advances.
solution: Parents log each advance in a simple app and tag it as gift, loan or advancement. The child e-acknowledges it. Optional interest at the AFR turns it into a formal promissory note. The system flags amounts near gift-tax-return thresholds (annual exclusion about $19K). It produces a running equalization statement the attorney can attach to a will or trust with a state-specific 'hotchpot' clause. An annual sibling-transparent 'family statement' replaces secrecy. Repayment or forgiveness schedules kick in when a child gets re-employed.
why_now: Millions of 22-35-year-olds face a low-hire market while Gen X and Millennial heirs are about to receive trillions (Cerulli: Gen X about $14T in the next decade). Federal student-loan caps reportedly tightened from July 2026 (verify), pushing more tuition onto family money. With a higher federal estate exemption (reportedly about $15M per person from 2026, verify), fewer estates are tax-driven and more are conflict-driven, so fairness documentation is now the main planning value.
revenue_model: $199 'Fair Share Package' (memo, ledger, 45-minute attorney review). $12-20/mo subscription. Attorney and RIA white label at $500/mo per firm or a per-household fee. Later: paid mediation add-on when siblings disagree.
non_obvious_insight: The AI jobs shock will show up in probate court a decade before it shows up in most statistics. Unequal parental support is the seed of the next generation of estate fights, and equalization is a data problem (a ledger), not a legal one. Parents will pay real money to keep their kids from fighting after they die.
first_30_days: With two friendly estate attorneys, draft an advancement memo and equalization clause for two states. Put up a landing page aimed at parents searching 'paying rent for my 26-year-old' and post in personal-finance and parenting communities. Sell the $199 package with a manual spreadsheet ledger to the first 25 families, then build the app around what they actually log. Ask 10 elder-law attorneys to co-present at seminars.

title: Forever Guardian: Lifetime Care After Parents Are Gone
one_liner: A prepaid, life-insurance-funded successor-care plan in which a named team becomes the lifelong advocate, money manager and care coordinator for an adult with a disability after the parents are gone.
customer: Parents in their 60s-80s of adult children with intellectual or developmental disabilities (nearly one million US households have adults with I/DD living with an aging caregiver). Referred by special-needs planning attorneys and financial planners.
problem: Parents dread 'who will look after them when we're gone.' Siblings are often unavailable, state Medicaid waiver waitlists are long, pooled special-needs trusts manage money but rarely relationships, and no single accountable person exists for decades. The current autism generation is about to become adults, and the adult cohort will surge.
solution: A tiered plan. (1) While parents are alive: a named care manager, annual home visit, a living 'letter of intent' binder (routines, medications, preferences), and monthly check-in calls, so the person already knows the successor. (2) At transition: the team acts as advocate or guardian-of-record where allowed, coordinates services, audits group-home quality, and works with a partner trust company holding a pooled special-needs trust. (3) Funded by a paid-up second-to-die life policy or an upfront fee plus a monthly retainer.
why_now: Peak-65 parents are hitting the age where the successor question is urgent, Medicaid home- and community-based services are under financial pressure, and adults with I/DD are living longer than any prior generation. It is a large, emotionally urgent market with no scaled, for-profit successor-care provider.
revenue_model: Upfront enrollment ($5-15k or insurance-funded), a monthly care-management retainer ($100-200), trust administration fees through the partner, and insurance commissions.
non_obvious_insight: The real product is a relationship that starts before the parents die. The annual home visit is both the moat and the sales funnel: by the time a parent passes, the guardian is already someone the adult knows and trusts. It converts a frightening legal product into a service with visible value every month while the parents are still alive to judge it.
first_30_days: Partner with three special-needs planning attorneys and one trust company. Sign 15 families to a $1,500 'Shadow Year' (assessment, letter-of-intent binder, quarterly visits, monthly calls). Hire one care manager and validate the guardianship, trust and licensing requirements for a single state before promising the full lifetime plan.

title: Funeral Home Land-and-Business Split Advisory
one_liner: An advisor that separates aging independent funeral directors' real estate from their operating business. The land goes to housing developers, the shrunken business is leased back or sold to a consolidator, and the advisor earns fees and a small equity slice.
customer: Owners of independent funeral homes (about 75% of 15,401 US funeral homes are family or privately owned), especially those over 60 without a successor. Infill housing developers and investors buy the land. Consolidators such as SCI and Everstory may buy the business.
problem: These sites were built for burial-era visitation: large buildings with big parking lots on prime corridors. With cremation at about 63%, flat deaths and volume down 1.4% at SCI, the buildings are oversized while taxes and upkeep rise. Owners get lowball offers for the business that bundle the land. Developers never see these parcels, which are off-market and not listed. The business buyer pool and the land buyer pool are disjoint and do not talk to each other.
solution: Screen parcels using zoning, lot size, transit and local cremation share, plus state licensing data on owner age. Offer owners a split: sell or ground-lease the land to a developer and lease back a compact 2,500-3,000 sf service footprint (or a ground-floor space in the new mixed-use building), or sell the business alone to a consolidator. Package parcels for states with single-staircase and missing-middle reforms. Sell paid feasibility studies first, then take closing fees and equity.
why_now: Single-staircase reform (7 states in 2025, Michigan in July 2026) and California AB 2074 lower infill costs. Rates near 7.5% make greenfield harder, so infill parcels gain appeal. Consolidator cash flow is strong (SCI operating cash flow up 43%), which makes them acquisitive. Cremation growth is making the buildings redundant.
revenue_model: $5-10K paid feasibility studies, a 2-3% success fee on the land transaction, 5-10% carried equity in the project, and a fee when the business is sold to a consolidator.
non_obvious_insight: Funeral homes are a large class of buildings whose function shrank while owners still think of them as businesses, not real estate. The highest and best use is often housing, and the key is to split the land from the operation so neither buyer pool discounts the other.
first_30_days: Pull funeral home parcels in two or three states with recent zoning reform. Contact 100 owners aged 60 or over (from state funeral-board license data). Sign three paid feasibility studies. Partner with one infill developer and one consolidator to test appetite.

title: Founder File for Under-18 Hustlers
one_liner: A verified business transcript, tax pack and Roth IRA earned-income record for the parents of teens who legally can't hold the seller accounts their income runs through.
customer: Parents of 14 to 17-year-old sellers (eBay, StockX, GOAT, Whatnot, TikTok Shop, Depop, Shopify), high-school entrepreneurship programs (DECA, FBLA, Junior Achievement, NFTE), and college counselors. $12 to $15 per month or $149 per year, or $5 per student through programs.
problem: Most major marketplaces require sellers to be 18, so teens run their business under a parent's ID and account. The income, cost basis and reputation all legally belong to the parent. The parent gets a 1099-K on gross sales with no cost basis, which looks like profit. The kid can't prove any of it on a college application, and nobody is documenting the earned income that would let the family fund a custodial Roth IRA (contribution capped at the lower of earned income or the annual limit, roughly $7,000 to $7,500 per year).
solution: Founder File connects read-only to platform exports, PayPal and Gmail receipts, matches purchases to sales for cost basis, and produces: (1) a signed Business Transcript PDF for Common App activity entries and scholarship applications, (2) a Schedule C-ready summary and quarterly estimates for the parent, reviewed by a partner CPA, (3) an earned-income letter and referral to Fidelity or Schwab custodial Roth accounts, and (4) an '18th birthday migration' kit to move history to the kid's own accounts.
why_now: The 2025 tax law rolled the 1099-K reporting threshold back toward $20,000 and 200 transactions, so many teen sellers land in a confusing gray zone about reporting. College admissions increasingly reward proof of real work as test-optional policies spread and AI-polished essays get discounted. Teen commerce through TikTok Shop, Whatnot and reselling is at its peak, and Gen Alpha hustle culture is pulling younger kids in.
revenue_model: Parent subscription, per-student pricing through school programs, and referral fees from custodial brokerage accounts. Possible upsell: CPA-reviewed tax filing.
non_obvious_insight: Teen resellers are among the most under-documented earned-income earners in the country. Documenting what they already do unlocks tax-free compounding worth thousands per kid and turns a bedroom hobby into an admissions asset. The buyer is the parent, who pays for college advantage without hesitation, while everyone else sells to the kid.
first_30_days: Recruit 30 teen resellers from the Discord servers I am in. Give them free transcripts in return for parent-approved testimonials. Have a CPA friend sign off on a template. Sell a $49 'Transcript plus Roth IRA setup' bundle to their parents, and offer the transcript to 5 college-counseling and 'teen entrepreneur' TikTok creators for an affiliate cut.

title: SLA-Backed Mirror of At-Risk Public Earth Data
one_liner: A paid continuity service that keeps free federal Earth-observation feeds flowing, with bridge products and an SLA, when the originals degrade or go dark.
customer: Crop and weather insurers, commodity and energy trading desks, hydropower and utilities, and reinsurers whose models ingest free NOAA, NASA and USGS satellite products.
problem: Free satellite and climate feeds have no SLA. Since 2025, reported budget pressure and retirements (DMSP-derived products, some NOAA archives) and aging flagship sensors (MODIS-era platforms nearing end of life) have exposed downstream firms to a single point of failure they never underwrote.
solution: A 'Data Continuity Desk': mirror the top 50 at-risk feeds, cross-calibrate substitutes (VIIRS, Sentinel-3, Landsat, commercial sensors) into documented bridge products, alert on schema and quality changes, and contractually guarantee delivery. Add an audit that maps each customer's model to its data dependencies.
why_now: The briefing notes NOAA and NASA EO budget cuts were not covered, so treat specifics as unverified. Prior knowledge points to 2025-26 funding fights and curtailed products. Meanwhile Sentinel and commercial sensors are mature enough to serve as bridges.
revenue_model: $2-50k per year per data product under SLA. $15-40k for a dependency audit. Enterprise bundles for insurers and trading desks.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders think free public data is a permanent public good. The businesses built on it hold an uninsured operational risk, and the seller who quantifies that risk and guarantees continuity gets paid like an insurer.
first_30_days: Inventory the 100 most cited NOAA, NASA and USGS feeds and score each for discontinuation risk. Publish the list, then call 30 insurers and trading desks and ask which feeds they run on. Build one bridge product, for example a snow or vegetation index, and sign two paid pilots.

title: WhatsApp Voice-Note Superintendent for Spec Builders
one_liner: A bilingual coordinator-plus-AI service that runs daily crew confirmations, headcounts and re-sequencing for a builder's two dozen subs over WhatsApp voice notes, priced per house.
customer: Small private and spec builders (20-300 homes a year) in Texas, Florida and the Southeast, and remodelers who juggle many subs.
problem: A typical home needs about two dozen subs. Foundations sit 30+ days waiting for crews, and one executive described 15-20 houses stuck 6+ weeks. Builders learn a crew is not coming days too late. Project software requires English typing and logins, and workers are wary of anything that looks like tracking. Procore's 20 agents serve larger GCs.
solution: Foremen keep sending Spanish voice notes on WhatsApp. The system transcribes them, extracts headcount, phase status and photos, and updates the schedule. A nearshore bilingual coordinator confirms tomorrow's crews by 5 p.m., calls backup crews when there is a gap, and sends the builder one exception report each morning. Privacy by design: counts and progress only, no IDs or location.
why_now: ICE arrests rose from 32,545 in May to 49,571 in July 2026. Crews can shrink overnight (a Minnesota roofing crew went from 80 to 6). Multilingual speech models and the WhatsApp Business API are mature, and PM incumbents are focused on big GCs.
revenue_model: $300-500 per active house per month, or $3-6K per month per builder. One coordinator handles 25-40 houses, so gross margin is high.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is not scheduling math, it is that the people who know whether tomorrow's crew is coming do not use the software. The interface must be the phone and language they already use. The daily headcount is the leading indicator, and knowing a day earlier lets a builder re-sequence trades instead of idling a foundation.
first_30_days: Sign 3 builders with 10-20 active houses each through a home builders association. Hire one bilingual coordinator. Run it manually with WhatsApp and a shared sheet, add speech-to-text in week 2, and document five saved crew-days.

title: Do-Not-Clone Voice Registry With Inference-Time Checks
one_liner: A privacy-preserving registry that voice-cloning vendors query before creating a clone, so voice actors and narrators can block or price unauthorized cloning at the moment of input.
customer: Voice actors, audiobook narrators and podcasters (and their agents) as enrolled voices, and TTS, dubbing, audiobook and podcast-tool vendors that pay for checks and compliance logs.
problem: YouTube's likeness detection is gated by agencies and celebrity status, with no path for long-tail creators, and its removals so far are 'very small.' State laws such as Tennessee's ELVIS Act and California's digital-replica statutes create liability for cloning without consent. Vendors want a cheap way to show good faith. Detection after distribution is a losing race.
solution: Enrolled voices are stored as one-way speaker-embedding hashes. Vendors call a check API with the reference clip before creating a clone. A match requires a proof-of-consent token that carries the owner's terms (price, banned categories). Owners get logs and payouts via vendor marketplaces. Start with voice actors enrolled through agents and narrators' communities, integrated with 2-3 mid-size TTS or dubbing vendors.
why_now: Likeness laws now exist in several places, the gap for non-celebrity creators is visible, speaker-embedding models are open, and vendors selling to enterprises need a compliance line item.
revenue_model: $0.002-0.01 per check plus $1-5k/month compliance tiers for vendors, per-talent annual fees from agencies, and a marketplace take rate.
non_obvious_insight: The money is on the liability side (vendors), not the creator side, and enforcement is cheapest at input (before a clone exists) rather than at output, where the detection war is being lost.
first_30_days: Build the registry and check API prototype. Enroll 100 voice actors through two agents and a narrators' Discord. Trial the check API free with five TTS and dubbing startups, aiming for a first paid compliance tier from a dubbing vendor.

title: Insurer-Funded Chronic Care for Diabetic Pets
one_liner: A tech-led diabetes and kidney-disease program for insured pets, paid per member per month by insurers who capture the avoided ER claims.
customer: Mid-size pet insurers and MGAs (for example Fetch, Pumpkin, Odie and Lassie-type carriers) that need to cut claim severity. Independent clinics are the referral partner, and self-pay owners are the fallback.
problem: Diabetes and kidney disease in cats and dogs generate $3-6K a year in claims and emergency DKA admissions. AAHA's 2026 guidelines emphasize CGMs and once-daily insulins, but the workflow of monitoring, titration, coaching and refills has no owner. Vets are overloaded, vet techs are 2 per vet against a 4:1 ideal, and insurers' premiums are up 19.7% against animals up 9%, so they need to reduce claim costs rather than only raise prices.
solution: Sell insurers a PMPM disease-management pod: CGM starter kit, weekly data review by licensed vet techs under a supervising vet via the owner's clinic, protocol-driven insulin titration messages, refill logistics, and early-warning routing to the clinic before DKA. Enrollment is found in the insurer's claims file. Clinics are paid a titration-visit fee so they are not disintermediated. Insurers pay $40-70 PMPM with shared savings on avoided ER events.
why_now: AAHA split canine and feline diabetes guidelines in 2026 and put CGMs at the center. CGMs and long-acting insulins are arriving at once. Ambient AI and the vet-tech underuse make labor arbitrage possible. Insurers face repricing backlash, and remote VCPR rules are loosening piecemeal.
revenue_model: PMPM from insurers, gain-share on avoided claims, and CGM sensor and supply margin. Owner self-pay at $59 a month as a fallback.
non_obvious_insight: Insurers sit on the only longitudinal dataset and carry the financial downside. Clinics hold the license but not the time. This is Livongo-style economics: the payer who owns the downside pays for prevention, and vet techs are the labor arbitrage. Chronic care is a claims-cost product, not a telehealth product.
first_30_days: Convince one small MGA to share a de-identified diabetic-claims cohort and pilot a 200-pet program at cost. Recruit two RVTs and a supervising vet. If insurers are slow, launch a $59 a month owner-pay version through 5 clinics to get outcome data within 90-120 days.
